title: Attributed Network Alignment: Combining Edges and Features
one_liner: When you have two similar networks and want to find which nodes correspond, using both edge connections and node features together beats using edges alone.
lead: You have two organization charts from different companies that merged. You want to figure out which person in the old chart matches each person in the new chart. Old methods only looked at how people were connected; they ignored the fact that each person also has skills, department, and salary — features that carry real signal about identity. When you combine edge patterns and features, you break ambiguities that edges alone cannot break, because two nodes must now match in two ways at once rather than one way. This paper shows how to do this and proves when and why it works.

problem.h2: Two graphs and no map between them
paras: You have two networks — maybe social networks, protein interaction graphs, or company hierarchies. They look similar, but shuffled. One network is an old version; the other is new. Every node (person, protein, entity) in the old network should match exactly one node in the new network, but you don't know which.

The naive approach: look only at the edges (connections). Find which node in the new graph has the same neighbor pattern as a node in the old graph. This works sometimes, but breaks when many nodes have similar patterns — you get stuck guessing, and ambiguity explodes. The reason: connection patterns alone give you only so much information to distinguish nodes.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence:
callout.html: Use both edge patterns and node features (attributes) together to pin down which nodes correspond, making the matching problem easier to solve correctly.

steps.text: Old and new network, each with edges and node features.
For each possible pairing of nodes, compute how well edges match and how close features are.
Weight edge evidence and feature evidence equally (or tune the balance) to rate each candidate matching.
Find the one-to-one mapping that maximizes total similarity across all node pairs, subject to the constraint that each node maps to exactly one other node.
Return which node in the new graph corresponds to each node in the old graph.

paras: Most graph alignment methods only use edge information. This paper adds node features to the matching process — it considers both the topology (how nodes connect) and the attributes (properties of each node) at the same time.

hidden.name: Minimum signal strength for correct matching
paras: Behind the scenes, there is a critical point: below a certain strength of correlation between the two graphs, no algorithm can figure out the right mapping, no matter how clever it is. This threshold depends on how many nodes there are and how much signal comes from edges versus features. The paper characterizes this threshold mathematically.

The paper measures this threshold by analyzing when a specific algorithm (quadratic programming) can recover the true mapping. It then proves that this threshold is optimal — meaning that no algorithm, no matter how clever, can succeed if the signal is weaker than this point, because the correlation between the graphs is simply too weak to distinguish the true matching from false ones.

heat.caption: Darker means the algorithm can solve the problem; lighter means it cannot. Features lower the threshold (make the problem easier).

reads.html: The paper proves: if your edge correlation is weak, features can push you over the edge into solvable territory. If both are weak, no algorithm works.
The authors establish optimal information-theoretic thresholds for exact and partial recovery in the featured correlated Gaussian Wigner model and show QPAlign achieves them.

mechanism.h2: Why using both edges and features works
paras: When you match nodes using only edges, you are betting that two nodes with the same neighbor count belong together. But in a large network, many nodes have similar counts — they look identical by edge pattern alone. Adding node features breaks ties: now two nodes can only match if they have the same edge pattern AND their attributes are close. A false match would have to agree in two independent ways at once, which is much rarer, because attributes and edges carry different information.

The quadratic program works by scoring every possible pair of nodes (old vs. new). It assigns each old node to exactly one new node to maximize the total score (a one-to-one matching). Because the score now combines both edge and feature evidence, the true pairing stands out more sharply against all the false competitors. The algorithm does not need to guess; the math forces it to find the global best assignment.

stages.s: Two graphs with edges and node features
Score each node pair on edge similarity
Score each node pair on feature closeness
Solve matching optimization to maximize total score

math.words: For each pair of nodes, compute edge and feature scores. Find the one-to-one assignment that maximizes the sum of scores across all matched pairs.
math.equation: maximize  sum_{i,j} ( S_edge(i,j) + S_feature(i,j) ) * assignment(i,j)  subject to each i mapped to exactly one j and vice versa
symbols: similarity score based on how edge neighborhoods match between node i and node j
similarity score based on how close the features (attributes) are between nodes i and j
1 if old node i maps to new node j, 0 otherwise
each old node matched to exactly one new node, and vice versa

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose old node A and new node X: edge similarity = 0.8, feature similarity = 0.7, combined score = 0.8 + 0.7 = 1.5.
Old node A and new node Y: edge similarity = 0.6, feature similarity = 0.5, combined score = 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1.
Old node B and new node X: edge similarity = 0.5, feature similarity = 0.6, combined score = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1.
Old node B and new node Y: edge similarity = 0.7, feature similarity = 0.8, combined score = 0.7 + 0.8 = 1.5.
Best assignment: A→X (1.5) and B→Y (1.5), total 3.0. Picking A→Y and B→X gives only 1.1 + 1.1 = 2.2. The algorithm chooses the first option.

math.note: The quadratic program searches over all possible one-to-one mappings and picks the one with the highest combined score.

charts.title: Edge-only alignment
charts.note: Using only topology means weak signal scenarios fail completely.

charts.title: QPAlign (edges plus features)
charts.note: Adding features pulls weak-signal cases into solvable territory. The threshold is lower; more problems become matchable.

items.html: If node features are random noise and uncorrelated between the two graphs, the algorithm still works but features add no help — you are back to edge-only performance, because random features make no true matches stand out (they are as likely to match random pairs as real ones).

If the old and new graphs record different attributes (old graph has salary, new graph has years worked), you cannot compare features directly. The algorithm assumes features are measured the same way in both graphs.
Quadratic programming scales with the square of the number of nodes. Matching a million-node network to another million-node network is computationally expensive, even with relaxation tricks.

Use features that are stable across the two networks, ensure the signal is reasonably strong, and use a solver that actually finds the global best matching. The theoretical threshold tells you whether a solution is possible at all.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small demo with two graphs of 20 nodes each. Add random edges to create correlation, then add random node features with varying signal strength. Run the edge-only baseline and QPAlign. Plot: how many node matches does each method get correct as you vary feature signal strength from 0 (useless) to high (very informative). Show that when features are strong, QPAlign wins because the second signal source breaks edge ambiguity; when edges are already strong, both methods work and the gap shrinks.
demo.closing: The demo must make it obvious that features act as a tiebreaker, lifting accuracy when edges alone are ambiguous.
